title: idle-fill and fairness calibration notes
content:
Purpose and quick summary:
This note captures an exploratory run of knobs around the continuous batching scheduler focusing on the "idle-fill" heuristics (partial batch early flush), fairness weight calibration across latency-sensitive vs throughput customers, and how these knobs interact with tail latency during microbursts. Goal is to find a small set of conservative defaults and a short checklist for per-cluster tuning.

Background and motivation:
- We have recurring customer reports of 200–400ms p99 regressions during short microburst traffic patterns even though p50/p95 look fine.
- Hypothesis: Small bursts create many tiny batches; the scheduler either waits for timeouts (raising latency) or flushes early (increasing small-batch penalty and harming throughput and cold-kernel inefficiency).
- There is a third axis: fairness demotion of throughput-tier tenants to prioritize latency-tier tenants — badly tuned, this amplifies jitter and produces tail amplification under congestion.

High-level heuristics investigated:
- idle_fill_enabled: allow scheduler to inject synthetic prefill from idle token budget to avoid single-request batches.
- idle_fill_threshold_ms: how long a queue must be idle before we attempt a speculative fill.
- early_flush_fraction: fraction-of-max-batch to trigger an early flush if waiting beyond a small grace window.
- demotion_decay and demotion_floor: fairness demotion curve parameters applied when tenant exceeds target latency budget.

Metrics to observe (primary):
- p50/p95/p99 server-side latency (end-to-end request enter->first-token and last-token), 
- scheduling delay distribution (time in queue before kernel dispatch),
- batching efficiency (mean batch size, variance),
- throughput (tokens/sec),
- cost proxy: GPU occupancy / kernel time per token,
- fairness metric: ratio of latency increase of throughput-tier tenants vs baseline under same load.

Instrumentation added for this run:
- microtrace tag inserted at queue enqueue and at batch-formation boundaries; emitted labels: tenant_id, request_type, sequence_len_est, early_flush_flag.
- histogramized enqueue->dispatch times (log-buckets) and per-batch composition snapshots (comma-separated small IDS).
- small synthetic workload generator (workload-lite) now includes a "microburst 90/10" profile: 90% background steady traffic at 40 RPS, 10% microburst spikes up to 1000 RPS for 3–6s every 30s.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Baseline: idle_fill_enabled=false, early_flush_fraction=0.9 (i.e., mostly wait), fairness default (demotion_decay=1.0).
- A: idle_fill_enabled=true, idle_fill_threshold_ms=2, early_flush_fraction=0.6, demotion_decay=0.8.
- B: idle_fill_enabled=true, idle_fill_threshold_ms=10, early_flush_fraction=0.5, demotion_decay=0.5.
- C: idle_fill_enabled=false, early_flush_fraction=0.4, demotion_decay=0.6, with token-budget backpressure tightened.
- D: speculative prefill (idle_fill) + strict fairness floor (demotion_floor=0.7) designed to protect throughput tenants.

Notes on workload isolation:
- Each run was a 30-minute replay of production traces for steady-state + the microburst-lite overlay.
- We pinned runs to the same machines and zeroed other background jobs.
- Collected 1s-resolution GPU occupancy and kernel timing from perf hooks.

Observed results (key findings):
- Baseline: p99 spikes to ~680ms during microbursts, mean batch size collapsed to 1.1 for ~5s windows, throughput dropped 12% due to kernel inefficiency.
- A (low threshold): p99 reduced to ~320ms, mean batch size during burst recovered to 4.2, but GPU occupancy dropped ~8% in steady state vs baseline due to extra scheduling noise; throughput overall neutral. Demotion decay 0.8 produced smoother latency for latency-tier tenants.
- B (higher idle threshold): p99 around 260ms but steady-state p95 increased ~30ms; larger idle threshold caused slightly longer queueing for non-burst requests. Demotion_decay=0.5 over-demoted and throughput-tier tenants saw 1.6x latency ratio under sustained load.
- C (no idle_fill, aggressive early flush): p99 unchanged, but cost-per-token improved slightly; however, fairness collapsed — latency-tier tenants benefited but throughput-tier tenants suffered large tail amplification.
- D (prefill + demotion_floor): best tradeoff for mixed-tenancy: p99 ~280ms, steady-state p95 stable, throughput-tier latency increase limited to ~10% under microburst. GPU occupancy within 3% of baseline.

Qualitative observations from traces:
- Early prefill reduces the number of one-off single-request batches but can cause short-lived contention on the prefill token pool when many tenants simultaneously attempt prefill.
- Demotion decay too aggressive makes time-to-recovery long after a burst — observed long tails for throughput-tenant requests minutes after end of burst in some runs.
- The most painful pattern is interleaved short requests (seq_len 8–16) mixed with a few long-context requests; kernel warmup and KV cache contention hurt observed latency beyond what scheduler knobs alone fix.

Hypotheses for root causes and follow-ups:
- Root cause likely a combination of (1) microburst arrival shaping creating many tiny batches, (2) demotion policies that react too strongly and stifle fair multiplexing, (3) prefill pool insufficiently isolated.
- Follow-ups:
  1) Implement per-tenant prefill budget windows (burst-token buckets) to avoid global prefill thrash.
  2) Add a short randomness jitter to idle_fill_threshold_ms per queue to avoid synchronized prefill.
  3) Tune demotion to be more proportional with a short cooldown timer to speed recovery.
  4) Instrument kernel-level cold-starts to separate kernel inefficiency vs scheduling delay in the profiling dashboards.

Quick recommendations (conservative defaults to try cluster-wide):
- Enable idle_fill with idle_fill_threshold_ms=3ms and early_flush_fraction=0.65.
- Set demotion_decay=0.75 and demotion_floor=0.6; add a 5s cooldown to demotion state.
- Add prefill token bucket per-tenant with 5 tokens refill interval 10s.

Risks and tradeoffs to call out:
- Prefill can reduce p99 quickly but increases scheduler churn/noise and may reduce GPU kernel efficiency if overused.
- Overly protective fairness gives latency tenants consistent experience but increases cost for throughput tenants and may harm tail under long sustained congestion.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Can we measure per-kernel cold overhead more precisely? (Need perf counters inside the runtime path.)
- Should prefill be prioritized by request estimated sequence length to reduce wasted speculation?
- Long-run: can we co-design model slicing (short-context fast path) with scheduler to avoid kernel inefficiency for short requests?

Immediate next steps (owners):
- Luca: prototype per-tenant prefill-token buckets and run A/B overnight (SRV-4221).
- Janelle: add jitter to idle_fill thresholds and push instrumentation to tracing pipeline (SRV-4223).
- Priya: create dashboard panels for kernel cold-start vs scheduling delay and draft a brief for SRE to validate cluster-level defaults.

Notes to self: keep this doc as the ephemeral field notebook; once we lock defaults, migrate summary to confluence and add a short playbook entry to runbook for on-call tuning checklist.

End of notes.
